name: PTY/TUI screen drivers for agents (agent-tui and peers)
tagline: Run any terminal app in a PTY; agent reads screen, sends keys

maintainability.bus_factor: low: each tool is a single maintainer or a small company side project
maintainability.summary: Many near-identical tools, each maintained by one person; activity has slowed for most after launch.

architecture.summary: All of them spawn the target program on a pseudo-terminal, feed its output into a headless terminal emulator (vt100/xterm-headless/pyte/vt10x/tmux), and expose verbs to the agent: launch, send keys/text/mouse, wait for text or idle, snapshot the screen as text (some also PNG), resize, kill. pproenca/agent-tui runs a daemon on a Unix socket managing sessions, with a CLI and a JSON-RPC WebSocket live preview. ConductorOne/agent-tui adds 'refs': a semantic outline of the screen with durable app-specific refs (@vim.mode, @vim.buffer) and generic positional refs (@e1), queried with a CSS-subset selector and waited on with `wait --ref`. mcp-tui-driver offers 23 MCP tools including ref-addressed clicks from a snapshot, asciicast recording, and a tui_run_code JavaScript scripting tool.
key_points: Works on any existing TUI with no cooperation from the app
Readback is the rendered screen (text, sometimes PNG), not the app's state
ConductorOne refs bring a DOM-like outline to terminal screens (agent-browser pattern for PTYs)

mcp-tui-driver tools: tui_launch, tui_close, tui_list_sessions, tui_get_session, tui_resize, tui_send_signal, tui_text, tui_snapshot, tui_screenshot, tui_press_key(s), tui_send_text, tui_click, tui_click_at, tui_double_click, tui_right_click, tui_wait_for_text, tui_wait_for_idle, tui_get_code_interface, tui_run_code, tui_get_input, tui_get_output

tui-mcp tools: launch, kill, list_sessions, status, resize, screenshot (PNG), snapshot (text), scrollback, output (raw bytes), read_region, cursor, send_keys, send_text, send_mouse, wait_for_text/idle/exit; plus a monitor TUI
mcp-tuikit: tmux-isolated sessions, txt/png snapshots, YAML flow runner
mcp-tui-test: stream (pexpect) and buffer (pyte) modes, pytest plugin, tui://{session}/screen resource

performance.summary: No published numbers; interaction is paced by wait-for-idle/wait-for-text polling.

agent_usability.how: MCP servers (tui-mcp, mcp-tui-driver, mcp-tuikit, mcp-tui-test) or a CLI the agent shells out to (both agent-tuis), with JSON output.
agent_usability.integration_effort: Minimal: one `claude mcp add` line or a binary install; the target app needs no changes.
agent_usability.readback: Screen text, cursor, scrollback, raw bytes, PNG screenshots; ConductorOne and mcp-tui-driver add a semantic outline with refs. App state is not visible, only what it draws.
agent_usability.granular_edits: None to the UI; the agent can only send input. Addressing is by screen position, text match or heuristic refs.
agent_usability.history: mcp-tui-driver records asciicast (.cast) with optional input; tui-mcp exposes scrollback; no seek/fork of application state.
agent_usability.summary: The universal fallback: an agent can operate any terminal program like a human, but it is scraping a picture of an app it cannot change or introspect.

score_notes.ui_as_data: UI is whatever the driven app draws; ref outlines are derived read-only data
score_notes.agent_drivable: full live operation (launch, keys, mouse, wait) but no creation or change of UI
score_notes.readback: text + PNG + semantic outline, but never the app's own state
score_notes.granular_edits: input only; no edits to UI
score_notes.time_travel: asciicast recording and scrollback, no state seek
score_notes.pixel_graphics: PNG capture is readback, not a graphics layer
score_notes.maturity: all under a year old with tiny usage

steelman: Screen drivers are the most universal answer to 'let an agent use a terminal UI': they need nothing from the app, so they work today on vim, htop, psql, k9s, lazygit, gdb, installers and every TUI ever written, including thc's own TUI and thc-scene. They hold long-lived interactive sessions that a bash tool cannot (a REPL in a transaction, an SSH login with 2FA), they return readable screens, and the best of them (ConductorOne's refs, mcp-tui-driver's ref-addressed clicks) are converging on a DOM-like accessibility layer for terminals, with selectors and wait-for-ref semantics that avoid flaky regexes. If the goal is merely 'an agent can see and drive a TUI', this category already solves it for free.
weaknesses: The agent sees pixels-as-text, not state; meaning is inferred from layout
Cannot change the UI, only press keys on it
Refs are heuristic or need per-app adapters (ConductorOne has adapters for vim, shell prompt)
Timing relies on wait-for-idle/text polling; flaky on animated or streaming screens
Fragmented: six-plus near-duplicates, each single-maintainer, low adoption (tens of npm downloads/week)
Unix-only for several (pproenca/agent-tui explicitly not Windows)

relation_to_scene.overlap: Agent sends keys/mouse to a live terminal UI and reads the screen back as text.
relation_to_scene.scene_reinvents: scene's `key`, `mouse`, `screen` socket ops duplicate what these drivers already do for any TUI, including scene itself. For black-box testing of scene, one of these is enough.
borrow: wait_for_idle / wait_for_text / wait --ref primitives for agents (scene can implement them exactly from its own state instead of polling pixels)
ConductorOne's ref grammar and CSS-subset selectors (@app.role[value=x]) for addressing scene nodes
read_region and scrollback ops on scene's screen
asciicast export of a scene session for sharing
A monitor TUI listing live sessions with attach (tui-mcp monitor)
relation_to_scene.gap_left: These tools cannot read app state, push or patch UI, bind data streams, add callouts, hot-swap the binary or rewind; scene is the cooperating app side that exposes structure instead of forcing scraping.
relation_to_scene.verdict_why: They drive any TUI from outside; scene is a TUI built to be driven from inside, and one of them is a good black-box test rig for it.
